ABSTRACT: Remote stereocontrol in transition-metal catalysis is a challenging but interesting research topic. In this work, we
achieved copper-catalyzed asymmetric yne-allylic substitution using electron-rich arenes and acyclic carbonates through remote
enantioselectivity control. The reaction delivers a variety of enantioenriched products that contain a diverse set of valuable moieties,
such as conjugated enynes, indoles, indolizines, allenes, and dihydrofurans, which are widely used in organic synthesis and act as key
units in bioactive molecules and natural products. The synthetic value of this protocol has been demonstrated in a series of further
transformations, and mechanistic studies have been conducted to gain more insight into the reaction.
KEYWORDS: copper catalysis, yne-allylic substitution, 1,3-enyne, electron-rich arene, remote enantioselectivity control
■
INTRODUCTION
The asymmetric construction of C−C bonds through remote
stereocontrol is a challenging but fascinating synthetic strategy
because it overcomes the limits of stereorecognition of remote
prochiral centers and has long been an object of great interest
in asymmetric synthesis. However, such a strategy is still
underdeveloped, especially in the field of transition-metal
catalysis.
1
In this situation, the Ru or Cu-catalyzed asymmetric
propargylic substitution has been established as a powerful
tactic for the formation of stereogenic centers having alkynyl
groups (Scheme 1a).
2
Recently, we disclosed the Cu-catalyzed
yne-allylic substitution using various stabilized nucleophiles
(Scheme 1b).
3
The key intermediate is a copper acetylide-
bonded allylic cation with a copper vinyl allenylidene species as
its resonance structure. The work systematically disclosed four
reaction modes between a diverse set of nucleophiles and
alkynylallylic carbonates and provided a blueprint for further
investigations. A subsequent mission is to develop the
asymmetric version of yne-allylic substitution, but it is a
much more challenging task because, besides the remote
stereocontrol to produce the desired α-substituted 1,3-E-enyne
product with a high level of enantioselectivity, two other
possible products, i.e., γ-substituted 1,4-enyne products and α-
substituted 1,3-Z-enyne products are also amenable to be
formed (Scheme 1b). Very recently, Lin and He reported the
Cu-catalyzed asymmetric alkynylallylic substitution using
amines as the nucleophiles, providing a series of 1,4-enynes
bearing amino functional groups (Scheme 1c).
4a
Soon after
that, Xu and Qi achieved the asymmetric Cu-catalyzed [4 + 1]
annulation using yne-allylic esters and cyclic 1,3-dicarbonyls.
The products are spirocyclic compounds (Scheme 1c).
4b
However, asymmetric yne-allylic substitution affording 1,3-
enynes via remote stereocontrol has not been achieved.
5
1,3-
enynes are key moieties in a myriad of natural products and
bioactive molecules,
6
and are also valuable building blocks that
have been extensively applied in various transformations
affording multiply substituted arenes, functionalized allenes,

7
but protocols
providing chiral 1,3-enynes bearing adjacent stereocenters still
remain scarce.
8
Considering the great importance of 1,3-
enynes, in this work, we describe the first highly regio- and
stereoselective yne-allylic substitution using linear carbonates
and electron-rich arene nucleophiles such as indoles,
indolizines, pyrrols, and 2-naphthols (Scheme 1d). The work
furnishes a variety of 1,3-enynes with heterocyclic moieties and
dihydronaphthofuran products with allene units. Three
reaction modes, i.e., monosubstitution, double substitution,
and an unprecedented [3 + 2] annulation, were disclosed. It is
noteworthy that a large number of drugs and pharmaceutically
active compounds contain heterocyclic rings such as indoles
and indolizines,
9
and allene structures widely exist in naturally
occurring substances and are used in organic synthesis.
10
Thus,
this work provides a convenient approach to make the above
molecules. Herein, we report the results.
■

Indolizines have been found as the key substructures in
many natural products and bioactive molecules, such as
lamellarin D, lamellarin N, indoxam, and butoprozine, and
promising anticancer, antidiabetic, and inhibitory activities
have been observed in artificial indolizine derivatives.
11
Therefore, we envisioned the possibility of employing
indolizines to yne-allylic substitution. Under the same
conditions used for indoles, we obtained the corresponding
product 5a in 79% yield with 96% ee (Scheme 2, 5a). Methyl
ester-substituted indolizine was compatible with the reaction
(Scheme 2, 5b), and the reaction also tolerated Me/Ph-
substituted indolizines (Scheme 2, 5c−5d). Furthermore, the
reaction using indolizine bearing a cyclic ketone moiety was
also proven to be successful, releasing 5e in a high yield with
an excellent ee value (Scheme 2, 5e). Then, we found that
both R

and R

donating and electron-withdrawing groups, and the reactions

carbonate having a tetrasubstituted alkene unit could also
deliver the corresponding product, albeit in a low yield
(Scheme 2, 5l).
The third mission of our study is to check the use of pyrrole
as the nucleophilic reagent. Pyrrole has been less employed in
the asymmetric allylic substitutions,
12
and only one asymmetric
propargylic substitution using pyrrole has been reported by the
Nishibayashi group,
2l
to the best of our knowledge. The
regioselectivity between N-substitution and C-substitution,
when pyrrole is used, is also an issue to be addressed. To our
pleasure, we found that double yne-allylic substitution
occurred, and the corresponding products were all obtained
with excellent 97−99% ee (Scheme 3, 6a−6d).
Having successfully achieved the asymmetric reactions using
a series of electron-rich heterocyclic arenes, we further
evaluated the fourth type of aromatic compound, i.e., 2-
naphthalenol (Scheme 4). To our surprise, a new reaction
mode that has been not disclosed previously was found, and

Further studies were conducted to obtain more mechanistic
insights into this asymmetric yne-allylic substitution. The
control experiment using 1a-Ph and indole 2a under the
standard conditions in Scheme 2 did not lead to any product
(Scheme 6a), demonstrating the importance of terminal alkyne
in the reaction. This was further demonstrated by the use of D-
labeled substrate 1a-d, and the reaction afforded 3f with D
atom lost during the transformation (Scheme 6a). The
relationship between the ee values of L4 and the ee values
of 5a shows a proximal linear kinetic profile, indicating that a
monomeric copper-allenylidene complex is probably involved
in the reaction (Scheme 6b). Similarly, the reaction producing
8a using ligand L1 also gives a linear correlation, showing that
a copper−ligand monomer complex possibly exists in the
mechanism (Scheme 6b). Further kinetic studies revealed that
the reaction was first-order on the Cu catalyst and zero-order
on both 1a and 2f (Scheme 6c). This further confirms that the
monocopper species is probably involved in the turnover-
limiting step.
The postulated mechanism of this asymmetric yne-allylic
substitution is described in Scheme 7. The yne-allylic
carbonate 1a first reacts with copper catalyst under base
conditions to give alkynyl copper intermediate Int-I, which
subsequently generates Cu-allenylidene intermediate Int-II
with a tautomer of Int-II’. Then, an outer-sphere nucleophilic
attack by electron-rich arenes occurs via remote enantiodiscri-
mination and finally generates products 5a or 8a′. An
intramolecular annulation happens for 8a′ under copper
catalysis and produces 8a as the final product.
■
CONCLUSIONS
In summary, asymmetric copper-catalyzed yne-allylic sub-
stitution using electron-rich arenes has been developed for the
first time, delivering a variety of 1,3-enynes bearing
heterocyclic ring moieties and allenyl dihydronaphthofurans.
The products contain a diverse set of valuable moieties, such as
conjugated enyne, indole, indolizine, allene, and dihydrofuran,
which are either key intermediates in organic synthesis or
important substructures in bioactive or natural substances. The
synthetic value of this protocol has been demonstrated in a
series of further transformations, and mechanistic studies show
that the ligands play a different role in delivering the products.
The work provides a new choice of achieving remote
stereocontrol via transition-metal catalysis and enriches the
toolbox for bioactive molecule discovery. Further investigation
of the novel application of asymmetric yne-allylic substitution
is ongoing in our group.
